clue.text: Short twisted shirt pressed by Chuck

indicators.note: the shirt is turned round, so its letters run backwards
the shirt is squeezed inside the word for Chuck

blocks.note: to chuck = to fling; it goes round the shirt
a tee = a T-shirt

explanation.surface: Someone's short, crumpled shirt has been flattened under a friend called Chuck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Short' looks like it describes the shirt; it is the definition, in its sense of brief. A tee is short for T-shirt, and chuck is the throwing sense, not a name.
explanation.definitionFit: Something fleeting lasts only a short time.

clue.text: Show American scoundrel iron masks

indicators.note: iron covers the other letters, holding them inside

blocks.note: Fe is the chemical symbol for iron; it goes round the rest
A = American
a cad is a man who behaves badly

explanation.surface: A rogue from America hides behind a disguise, as if at a masked show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Show' reads as a verb at the start of a sentence; it is the noun, a false display.
explanation.definitionFit: A facade is an outward show that hides the truth.

clue.text: Balance stock old skinflint unboxed

indicators.note: the box is the outside of the word, so the first and last letters come off

blocks.note: to stock a kitchen = to equip it
O = old
MISER without its outer letters M and R

explanation.surface: An account-book note: the stock balance of an old miser, taken out of its box.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Balance' and 'stock' both pull towards bookkeeping; 'stock' has to be read as a verb to give EQUIP.
explanation.definitionFit: Equipoise is an even balance of weight or force.

clue.text: Draws below gallery obscuring east side of Princes Street?

indicators.note: in a down answer, the draws sit under the gallery
the gallery hides east, so that letter is lost from it

blocks.note: TATE, the London art gallery, with its E dropped
a tie is a drawn match

explanation.surface: Someone sketches beneath a gallery that blocks the view of one end of an Edinburgh street.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Draws' looks like the definition, sketches below a gallery; it is only TIES. Princes Street is Edinburgh's main street, and tatties are Scottish potatoes, so they are a side dish there; the question mark flags the example.
explanation.definitionFit: Tatties, Scots for potatoes, are the kind of side dish you would be served in an Edinburgh restaurant.

clue.text: Ace possibly exchanging shilling for new brass

indicators.note: one letter is swapped out
gives what goes in: N takes the place of S

blocks.note: an ace in tennis is one kind of serve
s = shilling, the old British coin worth twelve pence; it comes out
N = new; it goes in

explanation.surface: A playing card, perhaps, traded for some new cash, with a shilling changing hands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brass' looks like more money beside the shilling; here it means cheek.
explanation.definitionFit: Brass is informal British for nerve, the cheek to do something bold.

clue.text: Process drug by fourth of October back in Stroud

indicators.note: take the fourth letter of October
take the letter at the back end of Stroud

blocks.note: meth = methamphetamine
O-C-T-O: the fourth letter is O
last letter of Stroud

explanation.surface: A drug case is processed by early October in the Gloucestershire town of Stroud.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Process' reads as a verb about handling the drug; it is the noun. Stroud is a small town in Gloucestershire.
explanation.definitionFit: A method is a process or way of doing something.

clue.text: Markets more IPA all over the shop

indicators.note: British slang for in a mess, so the letters are scattered

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 7 letters

explanation.surface: Shops are stocking more India pale ale everywhere.
explanation.walkthrough: The indicator is itself about shops, so it hides in the same picture as the definition. IPA is India pale ale, a strong hoppy beer.
explanation.definitionFit: Emporia, the plural of emporium, are markets or large stores.

clue.text: Dislikes promoting son’s expedition

indicators.note: in a down answer, promoting a letter moves it higher up the word

blocks.note: to dislike strongly = to hate
s = son, already the last letter of HATES; it moves up to third place

explanation.surface: Someone resents their son being pushed forward on a trip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Expedition' looks like a journey; it is the old sense of speed. The S only moves, so the letters are the same as HATES.
explanation.definitionFit: Expedition can mean promptness, doing something with haste.

clue.text: Drink enterprise supporting 500 northern hill folk

indicators.note: in a down answer, what supports sits below: the drink and enterprise go under the 500

blocks.note: D = 500 in Roman numerals
ale = beer
SME = small or medium-sized enterprise
N = northern

explanation.surface: A brewery business backing five hundred northern hill farmers.
explanation.walkthrough: The Dales are the valleys of Yorkshire in northern England, and a dalesman lives there, so 'northern' also fits the picture while giving N.
explanation.definitionFit: Dalesmen are the people of the Yorkshire Dales, hill country in the north of England.

clue.text: Left House powerless with party vote accepted

indicators.note: without P, the abbreviation for power

blocks.note: PORT (left, on a ship) + HO (house), losing P
a do = a party
X is the cross marked on a ballot paper

explanation.surface: A left-wing party that has lost power in the House has its vote accepted.
explanation.walkthrough: The political surface makes 'Left' and 'House' look like parliament; they are PORT and HO.
explanation.definitionFit: Orthodox views are the accepted, conventional ones.

clue.text: Player over on table with Jack nearly revised offer

indicators.note: in an across answer, player and over come after the table
the last letter is cut off

blocks.note: a counter is a table in a shop or kitchen
a prop is a front-row rugby player
O = over in cricket scoring
jack and salt both mean sailor; SALT loses its T

explanation.surface: A card player sets down a card at the table and, with a jack nearly played, makes a fresh bid.
explanation.walkthrough: The card-game picture makes 'Jack' a card; it is a sailor, as in jack tar, and so is a salt.
explanation.definitionFit: A counterproposal is an offer made in reply to another, revising its terms.

clue.text: Strip joint peeper periodically visits

indicators.note: something that happens periodically comes at regular intervals, so we keep letters at regular intervals: the second, fourth and sixth
the letters go into the joint

blocks.note: a dive is a seedy bar; it goes round the other letters
the even letters of pEePeR

explanation.surface: A voyeur keeps turning up at a strip club.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strip joint' reads as one phrase; the definition is 'Strip' alone, as a verb, and 'joint' is a dive.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym when used with 'of': taking away someone's rights strips them of those rights.

clue.text: Pole entering races alongside southern channel

indicators.note: the pole goes inside the races
the S is placed next to the rest

blocks.note: hares = races along, runs fast
N = north pole; it enters HARES
S = southern

explanation.surface: A Polish competitor enters swimming races down a southern channel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pole' has a capital to suggest a Polish person; it is a magnetic pole. 'Channel' looks like a waterway; it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Both verbs mean directing a force where you want it, as with the power of a river or your enthusiasm.

clue.text: Delivery of coat delayed application of plaster?

indicators.note: delivery is how words are spoken, so we hear the sound of the phrase

blocks.note: a fur is a coat; stayed = delayed

explanation.surface: A painter or builder complains that the coat of paint or plaster arrived late.
explanation.walkthrough: The plaster seems to be the builder's kind until you reach FIRST AID, where it is a sticking plaster on a cut; the question mark says it is just one example.
explanation.definitionFit: Putting a sticking plaster on a cut is a simple act of first aid.

clue.text: Cure last of meat eaten by drunk on a diet

indicators.note: take the final letter of meat
the T goes inside the rearranged letters
the letters stagger into a new order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 7 letters
final letter of meaT

explanation.surface: A dieter who got drunk tries to put right a lapse by eating meat.
explanation.walkthrough: Once the T is inside, the whole eight letters are rearranged together.
explanation.definitionFit: An antidote is a remedy, something that cures a poison or ill.

clue.text: Scottish town getting “unlimited” supermarket customers here

indicators.note: the word loses its limits, the letters at each end

blocks.note: PAISLEY, near Glasgow, loses its P and Y

explanation.surface: A Scottish town's shops have taken all limits off their customers.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a description, the place where shoppers walk. The quotation marks around 'unlimited' hint that the word is being used in an odd sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Supermarket customers walk the aisles between the shelves.

clue.text: Shift storage container close to covered entrance

indicators.note: the close, or end, of covered: its last letter

blocks.note: a spell = a shift of work
a bin stores things
last letter of covereD

explanation.surface: Someone moves a storage bin up near a sheltered doorway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Entrance' reads as a doorway; it is the verb, to en-TRANCE.
explanation.definitionFit: To spellbind someone is to entrance them, hold them fascinated.

clue.text: Trace element crudely recut

indicators.note: roughly made, so the letters come out rearranged

blocks.note: tin is a chemical element
RECUT rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone trying to trace an element that was roughly recut, like a gem or a key.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trace' reads as a verb, to track down; it is the noun, a slight hint of something.
explanation.definitionFit: A tincture is a slight trace or tinge of something.

clue.text: Model recalled gala edition covers

indicators.note: called back, so the letters read in reverse
the words cover the answer, holding it inside them

blocks.note: inside gaLA EDItion

explanation.surface: A special gala edition of a magazine featuring a model on the cover has been recalled.
explanation.walkthrough: The magazine surface makes 'covers' sound like front pages; it tells you the answer is covered by the words.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym as nouns: a perfect example to copy, as in 'a role model' or 'the ideal of good behaviour'.

clue.text: Space for members in extremely late train

indicators.note: the extremes of late: its first and last letters

blocks.note: first and last letters of LatE
to groom someone = to train them for a role

explanation.surface: Commuters complain about the lack of room for season-ticket members on a very late train.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Members' sounds like members of a club; they are limbs, legs in particular.
explanation.definitionFit: Legroom is space for your legs, which are members of the body.

clue.text: Messages fringing the Italian and English fabrics

indicators.note: the messages form a fringe around the other letters

blocks.note: texts = phone messages; they go round the rest
il is Italian for 'the'
E = English

explanation.surface: Messages trimming Italian and English fabrics, like labels sewn round the edge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fringing' belongs to the fabric picture as a trim; here it means surrounding.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: cloth made by weaving or knitting, the stuff of the textile industry.

clue.text: Contingent of Muslim men seizing monster

indicators.note: a contingent is a part of a group, so the answer is part of the words
the words hold the answer inside them

blocks.note: inside musLIM MEN SEizing

explanation.surface: A band of Muslim men captures a monster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Monster' reads as a noun at the end of the sentence; it is the informal adjective, as in a monster portion.
explanation.definitionFit: Monster used as an adjective means huge, immense.

clue.text: Inside of cage facing field Mike polished?

indicators.note: take the inner letters of cage
in a down answer, the pieces stand next to each other

blocks.note: middle letters of cAGe
a lea is a meadow
Mike is M in the NATO alphabet

explanation.surface: Mike has polished off the inside of a cage that looks out on a field.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark shows that polished is only one way to be agleam: something polished shines.
explanation.definitionFit: Something freshly polished is agleam, shining.

clue.text: Expected to cough up fish starters in gross Ely diner

indicators.note: the first letters of the three words

blocks.note: char is a fish of the trout family
first letters of Gross Ely Diner

explanation.surface: A disgusted diner in Ely, the Cambridgeshire cathedral city, is made to pay for fish starters he wanted to spit out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cough up' suggests being sick after bad fish; it is slang for paying. 'Starters' look like the first course; they are first letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A shop that charges you a price expects you to hand over the money; cough up is slang for paying reluctantly.

clue.text: It’s worth having agreement when knight’s lost

indicators.note: the knight's letter goes missing

blocks.note: assent = agreement
N = knight in chess notation; it is removed

explanation.surface: Advice that a deal is still worthwhile even after a knight drops out.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a description, not a synonym: an asset is anything worth having.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by description: a useful skill, person or possession counts as a valuable resource.

clue.text: Periodical girl brought back for interval

indicators.note: the word comes back on itself, read in reverse

blocks.note: Time is a weekly news magazine
gal = girl

explanation.surface: A magazine's cover girl is brought back after a break.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Periodical' looks like an adjective, now and then; it is the noun, a magazine.
explanation.definitionFit: A time-lag is an interval between one event and another.

clue.text: Broken bit broken by yours truly

indicators.note: the bit is split open and ME goes in the gap

blocks.note: a tad = a bit; it goes round ME
yours truly = the writer, me

explanation.walkthrough: 'Broken' appears twice; the first is the definition, in the sense of a horse that has been broken in.
explanation.definitionFit: A broken horse has been tamed, trained to accept a rider.

clue.text: Most plans run poorly by president playing unfairly

definitions.note: the answer is an adjective; the definition describes a player who is playing unfairly

indicators.note: badly made, so the letters rearrange
the president is placed beside the rest

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 12 letters
Ike was the nickname of US President Eisenhower

explanation.surface: A political comment: a president who plays dirty usually sees his plans go wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Run' belongs in the fodder, though it looks like the verb with 'poorly'. IKE joins the rearranged letters before they settle.
explanation.definitionFit: Unsportsmanlike conduct is playing unfairly, against the spirit of the game.

clue.text: Thumb maybe caught by Ben cycling in Bury

indicators.note: TOM is held inside the other letters
the first letter goes round to the end

blocks.note: BEN with B moved to the back; it goes round TOM
Tom Thumb is the tiny hero of an English folk tale; 'maybe' marks the example

explanation.surface: A man named Ben rides a bike through the Lancashire town of Bury with his thumb out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bury' is capitalised to look like the town near Manchester; it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: laying a body in a tomb is a burial.

clue.text: Bill and Ned retracted slander about PS?

indicators.note: drawn back, so NED reads in reverse
turned about, so the slander reads backwards

blocks.note: an ad, or advertisement, is a bill posted up
reverses to DEN
to throw mud is to slander; reverses to DUM

explanation.surface: Two men, Bill and Ned, withdraw a slanderous remark made in a postscript.
explanation.walkthrough: Bill and Ned look like two people; only Ned is a name, and Bill is an ad. The question mark shows a PS is one kind of addendum.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: a postscript is matter added at the end of a letter, one kind of addition to a text.
